questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Give a brief outline of the chemistry, diagnostic properties and crystallography of the following minerals:

(i) Zircon; (4 marks)

(ii) Olivine. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Zircon (4 marks).**

- **Chemistry:** zirconium silicate, $\mathrm{ZrSiO_4}$, a **nesosilicate** (island silicate) in which separate $\mathrm{SiO_4}$ tetrahedra are linked by $\mathrm{Zr^{4+}}$ ions. It often contains small amounts of **uranium and thorium** (replacing zirconium), which makes it very useful for **U-Pb radiometric dating**; the radiation may damage the structure (metamict zircon).
- **Occurrence:** a common **accessory mineral** of acid and intermediate igneous rocks (granite, syenite) and, because it is very resistant, a **heavy mineral in sands and sandstones**.
- **Diagnostic properties:** colour brown, reddish-brown, yellow, grey or colourless (rarely green); **adamantine to vitreous lustre**; streak white; **hardness about 7.5**; **high density (specific gravity about 4.6 to 4.7)**; no good cleavage, **conchoidal fracture**; transparent to translucent; very high refractive index and resistant to weathering and acids.
- **Crystallography:** **tetragonal system** (axes $a_1 = a_2 \neq c$, all at $90^\circ$); crystals are usually short **square prisms capped by pyramids** (dipyramidal habit), often small; knee-shaped twins are rare.

**(ii) Olivine (4 marks).**

- **Chemistry:** a magnesium-iron silicate, $(\mathrm{Mg,Fe})_2\mathrm{SiO_4}$, a **nesosilicate** forming a **solid-solution series** between **forsterite** ($\mathrm{Mg_2SiO_4}$) and **fayalite** ($\mathrm{Fe_2SiO_4}$).
- **Occurrence:** in **basic and ultrabasic igneous rocks** (basalt, gabbro, peridotite, dunite); it is the **first mineral to crystallise** in the Bowen discontinuous series, it does not occur with free quartz, and it weathers easily to serpentine, iddingsite and iron oxides. Gem variety: peridot.
- **Diagnostic properties:** typical **olive-green** (yellow-green to brown with more iron); **vitreous lustre**; streak white; **hardness 6.5 to 7**; specific gravity about 3.3 (forsterite-rich) up to about 4.4 (fayalite); **no good cleavage** (poor), **conchoidal fracture**; transparent to translucent; granular masses (crystals rare).
- **Crystallography:** **orthorhombic system** (three unequal axes $a \neq b \neq c$, all at $90^\circ$); crystals, when seen, are short prisms or tabular; mostly occurs as grains.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Write short notes on the following:

(i) Crystal twinning; (3 marks)

(ii) Parameters of a crystal; (3 marks)

(iii) Crystallographic axes. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Crystal twinning (3 marks).**

Twinning is a **regular intergrowth of two or more crystals of the same mineral** in which the parts are related by a symmetry operation that is not a symmetry element of the single crystal: **reflection across a twin plane**, **rotation of $180^\circ$ about a twin axis**, or inversion through a point.

- **Contact twins** (two halves joined along a plane): gypsum (swallow-tail twin), spinel.
- **Penetration twins** (crystals interpenetrate): staurolite cross, orthoclase (Carlsbad twin), fluorite.
- **Repeated (polysynthetic) twins:** many thin parallel twin lamellae, as in plagioclase feldspar (albite twinning, seen as striations or as black and white bands under crossed polars); cyclic twins are repeated around an axis (rutile, chrysoberyl).

Twinning may form during growth, by deformation or by inversion on cooling, and it is useful in **mineral identification** (plagioclase striations, microcline cross-hatching).

**(ii) Parameters of a crystal (3 marks).**

The **parameters** are the **lengths of the unit intercepts a, b and c** that a standard (parametral) face cuts on the **crystallographic axes**, and they give the **axial ratio** $a : b : c$ (with $b = 1$), together with the **interaxial angles** $\alpha$ (between b and c), $\beta$ (between a and c) and $\gamma$ (between a and b). They describe the shape of the unit cell and so fix the crystal system, for example cubic ($a = b = c$, $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^\circ$), tetragonal ($a = b \neq c$, all angles $90^\circ$), orthorhombic ($a \neq b \neq c$, all angles $90^\circ$). The intercepts of every other face are simple whole-number multiples of the parameters (**law of rational indices**), and their reciprocals give the **Miller indices** (h k l).

**(iii) Crystallographic axes (3 marks).**

- **Crystallographic axes** are **imaginary reference lines that pass through the centre of an ideal crystal**, along which the positions of the crystal faces are described. By convention the **c axis is vertical**, **a points towards the observer** (front to back) and **b goes from left to right**; each axis has a positive and a negative end.
- **Three axes** (a, b, c) are used for the cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic and triclinic systems; **four axes** are used for the **hexagonal (and trigonal) system**: three equal horizontal axes $a_1, a_2, a_3$ at $120^\circ$ to each other and a fourth, $c$, perpendicular to them.
- The **relative lengths of the axes and the angles between them** define the **seven crystal systems**: cubic ($a = b = c$, $90^\circ$), tetragonal ($a = b \neq c$, $90^\circ$), orthorhombic ($a \neq b \neq c$, $90^\circ$), monoclinic (three unequal axes, $\beta \neq 90^\circ$), triclinic (three unequal axes, no right angle), hexagonal and trigonal.
- *Sketch to draw:* three lines crossing at the origin (c vertical, b horizontal, a sloping toward the observer), labelled a, b, c with their positive ends, and the angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Distinguish between the following pairs of terms as applied in hydrogeology:

(i) Thermal spring and geyser; (2 marks)

(ii) Confined aquifer and unconfined aquifer; (2 marks)

(iii) Connate water and juvenile water; (2 marks)

(iv) Influent stream and effluent stream. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Thermal spring and geyser (2 marks).**

- A **thermal (hot) spring** is a natural outflow of groundwater **warmer than the surroundings**, flowing **continuously and quietly** at the surface. The water is heated by the geothermal gradient at depth or by hot igneous bodies.
- A **geyser** is a hot spring that **erupts periodically** as a jet of hot water and steam. It occurs in volcanic regions where water stored in a narrow, constricted channel is heated under pressure until part of it flashes into steam, throwing the water out; it then refills and the cycle repeats (for example Old Faithful, Yellowstone).

**(ii) Confined aquifer and unconfined aquifer (2 marks).**

- An **unconfined aquifer** is a permeable layer that is **not covered by an impermeable layer**. Its upper surface is the **water table**, at atmospheric pressure, and it is recharged directly from the rain falling on the surface above.
- A **confined (artesian) aquifer** is a permeable layer **between two impermeable layers** (aquicludes). The water is **under pressure**, so it rises above the top of the aquifer when a well is drilled (the piezometric surface lies above the aquifer, and a well may flow freely). It is recharged where the bed outcrops, often far away.

**(iii) Connate water and juvenile water (2 marks).**

- **Connate water** is **ancient water trapped in the pore spaces of sediments when they were deposited** (fossil sea water, usually salty), and it has stayed in the rock since.
- **Juvenile water** is **new water coming from the interior of the Earth** (released from magma), reaching the surface for the first time; it has never been part of the hydrological cycle and appears in volcanic and hot-spring areas.

**(iv) Influent stream and effluent stream (2 marks).**

- An **influent (losing) stream** has its bed **above the water table**, so it **loses water by seepage into the ground** and recharges the groundwater. It may dry up downstream and is typical of dry regions.
- An **effluent (gaining) stream** has its bed **below the water table**, so **groundwater flows into the stream** (base flow). It keeps flowing in the dry season and is typical of humid regions.
